hook.line: Thirty-two round pieces. By number of players it is counted among the world’s biggest board games — and the parks of China still buzz with games today.
hook.say: Welcome to the story of xiangqi!

ch.say: A river runs through the middle of the board.
p: Its origin is debated, including its link with India’s chaturanga.
Its modern form is thought to have settled in the Song dynasty (10th–13th c.), spreading to Korea and Vietnam.

ch.say: Over time, a cannon joined the army.
tl: The word “xiangqi” is old, but seems to mean another game
Xiangqi appears in a Tang-dynasty tale
The cannon is added — today’s form

ch.say: The general can’t leave the palace!
ch.cap: Pieces sit on the 9×10 points; the river is in the middle, the X marks the palace
p: Pieces stand on intersections and move along the lines.
The general and advisors stay in the palace; elephants cannot cross the river. The cannon captures by jumping exactly one piece.

cards: No river; the general starts in the centre of the palace
Pieces face down on half the board — luck plays a part
Tournaments across Asia and in Chinatowns worldwide
A legendary Chinese master who won the national title more than ten times from the 1960s
The words on the river recall the war between Chu and Han at the end of the 3rd century BC

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: Red or black — who moves first?
May the generals face each other?
No — facing each other on an open line is illegal
What do the pieces look like?
Flat discs, told apart only by the characters

p: Play on the same board as the park legends.
